Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LA PAZ, Bolivia (CNN)  -- Bolivian officials have declared a health emergency after three deaths attributed to dengue hemorrhagic fever, the often-lethal form of a mosquito-borne disease that more than 1,000 Bolivians are thought to have contracted since November. Brazilian soldiers pour insecticide to fight dengue fever in 2008. Bolivia also is battling the mosquito-borne disease. At least 12 unconfirmed instances of dengue hemorrhagic fever have been reported in the first 17 days of 2009, the official ABI news agency said. About 250 cases of dengue fever, the milder, nonlethal form of the disease, have been confirmed in the past two weeks, said Health Minister Ramiro Tapia in the Los Tiempos de Cochabamba newspaper. Authorities said they have committed more than 20,000 military personnel and 2.5 tons of insecticide to combat the disease. A preteen boy died last week at Children's Hospital of La Paz, a few days after arriving with internal bleeding, hospital director Christian Fuentes told La Razon newspaper in La Paz, the nation's capital. "By that time, there was nothing we could do. He had multiple internal hemorrhages," Fuentes said. A 17-year-old boy and a 30-year-old woman also died last week, the ABI news agency said, citing the national director of epidemiology, Juan Carlos Arraya. Cases of dengue fever usually spike from November through January, which is Bolivia's hot and rainy season. Alberto Nogales, the country's vice minister of health, said the fight against mosquitoes will last until April. Dengue occurs in tropical and subtropical parts of the world, transmitted by the bite of a mosquito infected with one of four dengue viruses, the World Health Organization says. Symptoms, which appear three to 14 days after the bite, can include mild to high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain and a rash, the WHO says. Dengue hemorrhagic fever is a potentially fatal complication that affects mainly children, the WHO says. Symptoms include fever, abdominal pain, vomiting and bleeding. The disease cannot be transmitted directly from one person to another. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates there are up to 100 million cases worldwide each year. "It actually is quite common," Dr. Ali Khan of the CDC told CNN last year. "And unfortunately, over the last 30 years or so we've seen an increase in the number of countries infected with dengue fever." Khan attributes the increase in part to population growth. Mosquitoes that carry dengue typically breed in areas near humans. "This is a disease that occurs where there's lots of population," he said. The WHO says mosquitoes carrying dengue viruses breed in exposed water, including places as shallow as jars, discarded bottles and plant saucers. Last year, 55,000 people in southeastern Brazil contracted the disease. The outbreak was confirmed as causing the deaths of at least 67 people -- almost half of them children under 13 -- and another 58 deaths were under investigation last summer, the Rio de Janeiro state's ministry of health reported at the time. Final statistics on the outbreak were not immediately available.

# Bolivia declares health emergency after deadly dengue outbreak

**LA PAZ, Bolivia — January 2009** — Bolivia declared a national health emergency after dengue hemorrhagic fever killed three people and thousands of suspected dengue cases were reported, health authorities said.

The emergency declaration allowed the government to mobilize additional medical staff, supplies and funding to fight the mosquito-borne disease. Officials focused their response on Bolivia’s tropical eastern regions, where warm temperatures and heavy rains had created favorable breeding conditions for the *Aedes aegypti* mosquito.

Authorities launched fumigation campaigns, removed standing water and urged residents to cover water containers and seek medical care if they developed symptoms such as high fever, severe headache, joint pain or rash.

Dengue hemorrhagic fever is a severe form of dengue that can cause internal bleeding, circulatory failure and death. Health officials warned that patients showing signs of bleeding, persistent vomiting or intense abdominal pain required immediate treatment.

The government also stepped up monitoring in hospitals and clinics as officials worked to contain the outbreak and prevent further deaths.

## Bolivia dengue outbreak report

**Situation as of late February–early March 2023:** Bolivia recorded **more than 8,700 laboratory-confirmed dengue cases**, while health authorities were investigating **over 19,000 suspected cases**. At least **29 deaths** were attributed to the outbreak. Santa Cruz, the country’s most populous department, was the main center of transmission, with hospitals facing heavy pressure and many infections occurring among children.

### Government and military response

The Bolivian government deployed approximately **3,000 members of the armed forces** to Santa Cruz and other affected areas. Working with health teams, troops:

- Went house to house looking for mosquito-breeding sites.
- Removed standing water, discarded tires and other containers.
- Helped clean neighborhoods and public spaces.
- Supported insecticide spraying and public-awareness campaigns.

The response focused on controlling *Aedes* mosquitoes, which breed in small collections of water around homes and transmit dengue during the daytime.

### WHO background

The **World Health Organization** describes dengue as a mosquito-borne viral infection common in tropical and subtropical regions. It estimates that **100 million to 400 million infections occur globally each year**, although many cause no symptoms or only mild illness.

Typical symptoms include high fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea and rash. A small proportion of patients develop **severe dengue**, which can cause bleeding, shock, organ impairment and death. There is no specific antiviral treatment; early diagnosis, careful monitoring and fluid management reduce mortality.

### CDC background

The **U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention** says dengue is caused by four related viruses and is spread mainly by infected *Aedes aegypti* mosquitoes. About **one in four infected people becomes ill**, and roughly **one in 20 symptomatic patients develops severe dengue**.

The CDC advises urgent medical care for warning signs such as:

- Severe abdominal pain
- Persistent vomiting
- Bleeding from the nose or gums
- Blood in vomit or stool
- Extreme tiredness or restlessness

Prevention centers on avoiding mosquito bites and eliminating standing water. Because anti-inflammatory medicines such as aspirin and ibuprofen can increase bleeding risk, the CDC generally recommends acetaminophen/paracetamol for fever while seeking medical guidance.

*Case and fatality totals changed as surveillance continued; the figures above reflect reporting during the major 2023 outbreak response.*

**Bolivia’s 2009 dengue epidemic exposed regional vulnerability to resurgent virus**

**LA PAZ, Bolivia —** Bolivia’s worst recorded dengue fever crisis swept through the country’s tropical lowlands in early 2009, overwhelming hospitals, prompting a national emergency and exposing weaknesses in mosquito control and public-health surveillance. The epidemic followed another major outbreak a year earlier in southeastern Brazil, where dengue killed scores of people and placed extraordinary pressure on hospitals in Rio de Janeiro state.

Bolivian health authorities recorded more than 57,000 suspected infections during the 2009 epidemic, with several thousand cases confirmed by laboratory testing and about 25 deaths reported, according to government and Pan American Health Organization figures from the period. Although reporting standards varied and many mild infections never reached clinics, the totals made it the largest dengue outbreak Bolivia had documented.

The eastern department of Santa Cruz, Bolivia’s most populous lowland region and its commercial farming center, bore the brunt of the epidemic. Cases also appeared in Beni, Pando, Tarija, Chuquisaca and the tropical areas of Cochabamba and La Paz departments.

President Evo Morales declared a national health emergency in February 2009, allowing the government to direct additional personnel, insecticides, diagnostic supplies and hospital resources toward affected areas. Medical brigades, including Cuban doctors working in Bolivia, joined local teams treating patients and conducting neighborhood campaigns.

Workers fumigated homes, sprayed streets and urged residents to empty water from discarded tires, barrels, flowerpots and other containers where *Aedes aegypti* mosquitoes breed. The mosquito, which also transmits yellow fever, Zika and chikungunya, thrives in densely populated urban areas where water storage is common and garbage collection or drainage is inadequate.

Dengue usually causes high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint aches, nausea and rash. A smaller proportion of patients develop severe dengue—then widely called dengue hemorrhagic fever—which can produce internal bleeding, circulatory collapse and death. There is no specific antiviral treatment; prompt monitoring, careful fluid replacement and rapid treatment of shock are critical.

Bolivia’s crisis was intensified by heavy seasonal rains and warm temperatures, which created abundant breeding sites. Rapid urban growth around Santa Cruz and other lowland cities complicated eradication efforts. Public-health officials also warned that simultaneous circulation of multiple dengue virus serotypes increased the danger of severe illness among people who had previously been infected with a different strain.

The epidemic drew inevitable comparisons with the outbreak that struck southeastern Brazil in 2008, especially Rio de Janeiro state. Brazilian authorities reported more than 700,000 suspected dengue cases nationwide that year and more than 200 deaths. Rio state alone registered roughly a quarter-million cases and about 170 deaths, with children accounting for an unusually large share of severe cases and fatalities.

In Rio, emergency rooms and pediatric wards were inundated. The Brazilian government deployed military personnel to help operate field hospitals, distribute information and eliminate standing water. Long lines formed outside clinics as residents sought blood tests and treatment, while officials faced criticism that mosquito-control programs had been relaxed after earlier declines in case numbers.

The Brazilian epidemic was closely associated with the renewed circulation of dengue virus serotype 2 in a population whose immunity had been shaped by previous waves of other serotypes. Epidemiologists said that pattern contributed to severe disease, particularly among younger patients who had little prior exposure to serotype 2.

Bolivia’s 2009 outbreak was smaller than Brazil’s in absolute numbers, reflecting Bolivia’s much smaller population. Proportionally, however, it represented a major national emergency. Bolivia had about 10 million inhabitants at the time, compared with nearly 190 million in Brazil, and possessed fewer intensive-care beds, laboratories and specialist services.

The epidemics also differed geographically. Brazil’s 2008 crisis struck one of Latin America’s largest metropolitan areas, with densely packed neighborhoods and extensive hospital networks that were nevertheless pushed beyond capacity. Bolivia’s epidemic was concentrated in lower-altitude tropical regions, often far from the country’s political center in La Paz. Mountainous western cities were largely protected by cooler temperatures and elevations unfavorable to *Aedes aegypti*, but distance and uneven infrastructure made it difficult to move staff and supplies to affected departments.

Both outbreaks demonstrated the limits of emergency fumigation. Spraying can kill adult mosquitoes, but it has little lasting effect if eggs and larvae remain in household water containers. Health specialists stressed that durable control required regular garbage collection, reliable piped water, covered storage tanks, community inspections and year-round surveillance—not only campaigns after hospitals began filling.

They also illustrated a recurring regional pattern: dengue cases often fell after a major epidemic, encouraging authorities and residents to lower their guard, only to surge again when weather conditions, mosquito populations and viral immunity aligned.

For Bolivia, the 2009 epidemic became a warning that dengue was no longer an occasional tropical nuisance but a persistent national health threat. Brazil’s experience the previous year had already shown that greater wealth and a larger medical system offered no guarantee against catastrophe. In both countries, the virus exploited the same vulnerabilities—crowded cities, standing water, inconsistent prevention and populations with uneven immunity—to turn seasonal transmission into a public-health emergency.

counterfactuals.output:
## Bolivia mobilizes military and insecticide in campaign against dengue

Bolivian authorities deployed more than 20,000 military personnel and distributed about 2.5 tons of insecticide as part of an emergency campaign to contain dengue, a mosquito-borne disease that can cause severe illness and death.

The large-scale mobilization reflects the difficulty of controlling an outbreak once the virus is circulating widely. Troops can quickly reach affected neighborhoods to fumigate homes and public spaces, remove rubbish, drain standing water and help health workers identify areas with high numbers of infections. The insecticide is intended mainly to kill adult mosquitoes, reducing the immediate risk of further transmission.

Warm temperatures and seasonal rains create ideal conditions for *Aedes aegypti*, the mosquito that spreads dengue. Its eggs and larvae develop in stagnant water, often in or around people’s homes. Common breeding sites include uncovered water tanks, barrels, buckets, discarded tires, flowerpots, roof gutters, bottles, cans and any other container that can collect rainwater.

Dengue is transmitted when a female *Aedes* mosquito bites a person infected with the virus and later bites someone else. It generally does not spread directly from person to person. The mosquitoes are most active during the day, particularly in the early morning and late afternoon.

Symptoms usually begin several days after an infected bite and can include:

- Sudden high fever  
- Severe headache  
- Pain behind the eyes  
- Muscle, bone and joint pain  
- Nausea or vomiting  
- Skin rash  
- Fatigue  

Most patients recover with rest, fluids and medical monitoring. However, some develop severe dengue, which may involve bleeding, breathing difficulty, intense abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, organ damage or a dangerous fall in blood pressure. People with warning signs should seek urgent medical care. Aspirin and ibuprofen are generally avoided because they can increase bleeding risk; health professionals commonly recommend paracetamol for fever and pain when appropriate.

Fumigation can suppress adult mosquito populations, but its effect is temporary if breeding sites remain. That is why the military operation also emphasizes household inspections and the removal or covering of water containers. Residents are typically urged to use mosquito repellent, wear clothing that covers the skin, install window screens and regularly scrub containers in which mosquitoes may lay eggs.

By combining insecticide spraying with a broad cleanup effort, Bolivia aims to interrupt transmission rapidly while reducing the places where the next generation of mosquitoes can develop.

## Three reported dead from severe dengue in Bolivia as health authorities warn of wider regional surge

**LA PAZ, Bolivia —** Three people have died after developing dengue hemorrhagic fever in Bolivia, according to reports from the state-run **Bolivian Information Agency, or ABI, and local newspapers citing health officials**.

Authorities said the deaths were associated with the most dangerous form of the mosquito-borne disease, which can cause internal bleeding, circulatory failure and shock. Officials were investigating the patients’ clinical histories and intensifying mosquito-control and disease-surveillance efforts in affected communities, according to the reports.

The exact location, dates and identities of the three victims should be confirmed against the original ABI dispatch and the relevant departmental health service before publication. Bolivian newspapers including **El Deber, La Razón and Los Tiempos** regularly obtain local dengue figures from departmental health services, known as SEDES, but their totals can differ depending on when the data were collected and whether deaths are listed as suspected or laboratory-confirmed.

### What “dengue hemorrhagic fever” means

The World Health Organization no longer relies primarily on the older categories of “dengue fever” and “dengue hemorrhagic fever.” Under WHO guidance introduced in 2009, cases are generally classified as:

- dengue without warning signs;
- dengue with warning signs; or
- severe dengue.

Severe dengue can involve major bleeding, severe plasma leakage leading to shock or respiratory distress, or serious organ impairment.

Most dengue infections are mild or asymptomatic. Patients who become ill commonly experience high fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea or rash. Warning signs often appear as the fever subsides and can include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, extreme fatigue, restlessness, rapid breathing or pale and cold skin.

WHO advises people with possible warning signs to obtain urgent medical care. There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue, but early recognition, careful monitoring and appropriate fluid management substantially reduce the risk of death from severe disease.

Health agencies caution against taking aspirin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as ibuprofen, when dengue is suspected because they may increase bleeding risk. Acetaminophen, also known as paracetamol, is generally recommended for fever and pain when medically appropriate.

### A disease spread by urban mosquitoes

Dengue is caused by four closely related viruses and is transmitted mainly by infected female *Aedes aegypti* mosquitoes. The mosquitoes thrive near people and breed in small collections of standing water, including uncovered tanks, discarded tires, flowerpots, buckets and household containers.

Bolivian health authorities typically respond to outbreaks by eliminating breeding sites, applying larvicides, fumigating areas with active transmission and urging residents to use repellents, screens and clothing that covers the arms and legs. Fumigation can kill adult mosquitoes but does not replace the removal of standing water, public-health specialists say.

Because Bolivia includes tropical and subtropical areas favorable to *Aedes* mosquitoes, transmission is often concentrated in lower-altitude departments, including Santa Cruz, Beni, Pando, Cochabamba, Tarija and northern La Paz. Local conditions, however, vary, and any geographic attribution connected with the three deaths requires confirmation from Bolivia’s Ministry of Health or the relevant SEDES office.

### Global and regional burden

Dengue has expanded dramatically worldwide over recent decades. The **US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention** estimates that as many as **400 million people are infected each year**, that roughly **100 million become ill**, and that about **40,000 die from severe dengue**. The estimates include infections that are never diagnosed or officially reported.

WHO similarly estimates **100 million to 400 million infections annually** and says about half of the world’s population is at risk.

The Americas have experienced an unprecedented rise in dengue. According to the **Pan American Health Organization**, the region recorded **more than 4.5 million reported cases in 2023**. In **2024**, countries in the Americas reported **more than 13 million suspected cases and over 8,000 deaths**, making it the region’s largest recorded dengue epidemic. Brazil accounted for most cases, but substantial outbreaks also affected Argentina, Paraguay, Peru, Colombia, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.

Regional totals are not directly comparable with Bolivia’s confirmed case count. PAHO figures may combine suspected, probable and confirmed cases, and reporting delays can cause national and regional databases to differ.

### Climate and immunity contribute to outbreaks

Dengue epidemics are shaped by multiple factors, including rainfall, heat, water-storage practices, urban growth, mosquito-control coverage and the circulation of different viral serotypes. Higher temperatures can accelerate mosquito development and viral replication, while heavy rain can create breeding sites. Drought can also increase risk when households store water in uncovered containers.

Infection with one dengue serotype generally produces long-term protection against that serotype but not against the other three. A later infection with a different serotype may increase the risk of severe disease in some patients, although severe dengue can occur during any infection.

Children, pregnant people, older adults and people with underlying health conditions may require especially close monitoring. Previous dengue infection can also be clinically significant.

### Vaccine policy requires local guidance

Two dengue vaccines have been authorized in some countries, but recommendations vary. WHO has recommended the TAK-003 vaccine, marketed as Qdenga in some jurisdictions, for children ages 6 to 16 in high-transmission settings under specified conditions. The older Dengvaxia vaccine is generally restricted to people with laboratory evidence of a previous dengue infection because of the risk of severe illness in recipients who had never been infected.

Bolivians should follow the Ministry of Health’s current vaccination and eligibility guidance rather than assuming that a vaccine approved elsewhere is available or recommended locally.

### Source note

This report draws on the following source categories:

- **ABI**, Bolivia’s state news agency, for the report of three deaths and official statements;
- Bolivian newspapers such as **El Deber, La Razón and Los Tiempos**, which report departmental dengue figures and remarks from SEDES officials;
- **Bolivia’s Ministry of Health and Sports** and departmental health services for epidemiological confirmation;
- **WHO**, *Dengue and severe dengue*, for symptoms, clinical classification and treatment guidance;
- **CDC**, *About Dengue* and global burden estimates;
- **PAHO**, regional dengue surveillance dashboards and epidemiological updates.

**Editorial caution:** The prompt does not specify the date, department, victims or source links for the three deaths. Those details should not be added without the original ABI article, local newspaper reports and an official Bolivian epidemiological bulletin. The deaths should also be described as “reported,” rather than confirmed, unless the Ministry of Health or a SEDES authority has formally validated them.
